questions.question: How do you optimize Redis memory usage and configure eviction policies for a production Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Redis Memory Optimization: Eviction Policies and maxmemory Configuration
questions.direct_answer: Redis memory optimization combines the right eviction policy, appropriate data structure choices, key expiry discipline, and maxmemory limits. The eviction policy determines what Redis does when it hits its memory limit — allkeys-lru evicts the least-recently-used key regardless of TTL, while volatile-lru only evicts keys that have a TTL set. For a cache-only Redis, allkeys-lru is the standard choice; for a mixed cache and persistent data store, volatile-lru protects keys without TTLs from eviction.

interviewer_intent.testing: Operational awareness of Redis memory management, eviction policies, and the implications of hitting maxmemory for application behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not setting maxmemory at all, allowing Redis to consume all available RAM and trigger OOM kills, or using the default noeviction policy with a cache workload.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Redis's memory encoding optimizations (ziplist/listpack for small collections), the OBJECT ENCODING command to inspect encodings, and Redis 7's listpack replacing ziplist.

sections.title: Memory management: the operational backbone of production Redis
sections.content:
Redis stores everything in RAM, so memory management is not optional — it is the most critical operational concern. Without a `maxmemory` setting, Redis will consume all available RAM until the operating system's OOM killer terminates the process, causing an unplanned outage. Setting `maxmemory` to 70–80% of available RAM leaves headroom for the OS page cache, replication buffers, and the memory overhead of `BGSAVE`/`BGREWRITEAOF` forks (which can temporarily double memory usage via copy-on-write).

The eviction policy determines what happens when Redis hits the memory ceiling. The default `noeviction` policy returns an error on write commands, which is appropriate for session stores or queues where silent data loss is unacceptable. For pure caches, `allkeys-lru` is the standard: it evicts the least recently used key from the entire keyspace. `allkeys-lfu` (least frequently used) performs better under power-law access distributions where a small set of hot keys should never be evicted despite being accessed less recently than a burst of cold keys. `volatile-lru` and `volatile-lfu` restrict eviction to keys that have a TTL set, which is useful when Redis serves as both a cache (keys with TTL) and a persistent store (keys without TTL).

Beyond eviction policy, data structure choice is the biggest memory lever. Redis uses compact internal encodings — listpack (replacing ziplist in Redis 7) — for small Hashes, Lists, Sets, and ZSets. A Hash with fewer than `hash-max-listpack-entries` (128 by default) fields uses a flat array that consumes roughly 10× less memory than a full hash table. Storing a user's attributes as one Hash instead of N separate String keys saves both the per-key overhead (~70 bytes each) and enables the compact encoding. Monitoring `OBJECT ENCODING <key>` and `MEMORY USAGE <key>` helps identify keys that have outgrown their compact encoding.

Serialization format also matters: JDK serialization stores class metadata and is 2–3× larger than JSON, which is in turn larger than binary formats like Protobuf or Kryo. For high-cardinality caches, switching serializers can reduce Redis memory by 30–50%. Combine compact serialization with short key names (abbreviate when key count is in the millions) and mandatory TTLs on every key to keep memory predictable.

sections.title: Eviction Policies Explained
sections.content:
Redis offers 8 eviction policies, grouped by scope:

**All-keys policies** (operate on the entire keyspace):
- **`allkeys-lru`** — Evicts the least recently used key. Best for general-purpose caching where you want hot data retained.
- **`allkeys-lfu`** — Evicts the least frequently used key. Better than LRU when access follows a power-law distribution (few very hot keys).
- **`allkeys-random`** — Evicts a random key. Fast but unpredictable — rarely the right choice.

**Volatile policies** (only evict keys with a TTL set):
- **`volatile-lru`** — LRU among keys with `EXPIRE`. Protects keys without TTL from eviction.
- **`volatile-lfu`** — LFU among keys with `EXPIRE`.
- **`volatile-random`** — Random eviction among keys with `EXPIRE`.
- **`volatile-ttl`** — Evicts the key closest to expiration. Useful when short-TTL keys are least valuable.

**No eviction:**
- **`noeviction`** (default) — Returns an error on writes when `maxmemory` is reached. Appropriate for session stores or queues where silent data loss is unacceptable.

**Decision framework:**
- Pure cache → `allkeys-lru` or `allkeys-lfu`
- Mixed cache + persistent data → `volatile-lru` (protects persistent keys)
- Session store → `noeviction` (fail loudly, don't lose sessions)
- Short-lived data → `volatile-ttl` (evict nearest-to-expire first)

sections.title: Redis Memory Configuration
sections.content:
```bash
# redis.conf — Memory management
maxmemory 6gb                       # 70-80% of available RAM
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru        # Evict least recently used
maxmemory-samples 10                # Sample size for LRU approximation (default 5)

# Lazy eviction — free memory in background thread
lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes
lazyfree-lazy-expire yes
lazyfree-lazy-server-del yes

# Compact encoding thresholds
hash-max-listpack-entries 128       # Hash uses listpack below this field count
hash-max-listpack-value 64          # Hash uses listpack below this value size
list-max-listpack-size -2           # ~8 KB per listpack node
zset-max-listpack-entries 128
zset-max-listpack-value 64
set-max-intset-entries 512
```

Monitor memory usage and eviction rates:

```bash
# Check current memory stats
redis-cli INFO memory | grep -E "used_memory_human|maxmemory_human|mem_fragmentation"

# Watch eviction rate in real-time
redis-cli INFO stats | grep evicted_keys

# Inspect encoding of a specific key
redis-cli OBJECT ENCODING user:42
redis-cli MEMORY USAGE user:42
```

sections.title: Memory Optimization Tips in Java
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`allkeys-lru` for pure caches** — evicts least recently used key regardless of TTL; the right default when all cached data has equal priority and memory is the bottleneck
- **`volatile-lru` for mixed persistent and cache data** — only evicts keys with TTL set; protects persistent data (sessions, locks) from eviction when used on the same Redis instance as cache data
- **`noeviction` for queues and session stores** — rejects writes when memory is full; requires capacity monitoring and alerting; prevents silent data loss at the cost of write failures
- **Hash encoding with ziplist saves memory** — keep Hash fields below 128 and values short to stay in compact ziplist encoding; one Hash key with N fields uses less memory than N separate String keys
- **`MEMORY USAGE key` and `MEMORY DOCTOR`** — diagnose memory consumption per key and get a Redis-generated diagnosis of memory pressure causes; run before scaling up instance size

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Memory management is one of the most operationally important aspects of running Redis in production. Redis stores all data in RAM, so running out of memory stops it from accepting new writes — and the eviction policy determines what happens at that point.

**Eviction policies — what to evict when memory is full**
- `allkeys-lru` evicts the least recently used key across all keys — the right default for a cache where all data has equal priority; Redis automatically removes cold data as memory fills
- `volatile-lru` evicts the LRU key only among keys with a TTL set — protects keys without TTL from eviction; useful when the same Redis instance holds both cached data (TTL set) and persistent data (no TTL)
- `noeviction` rejects new writes with an error when memory is full — appropriate for a session store or queue where losing any data would be catastrophic; requires monitoring to prevent hitting the limit
- `allkeys-lfu` evicts the least frequently used key — better than LRU for access patterns where old keys are still popular; Redis 4.0+

**Data structure choices affect memory**
- A Hash with fewer than 128 fields and small values is stored as a compact ziplist in memory — much more memory-efficient than storing each field as a separate String key; `HSET user:123 name Alice email alice@example.com` uses less memory than `SET user:123:name Alice` + `SET user:123:email alice@example.com`
- Lists, Sets, and Sorted Sets also use compact encoding below configured size thresholds; stay below `hash-max-listpack-entries` (128) to keep ziplist encoding

**Key expiry and memory pressure**
- Redis expires keys lazily (checked on access) and actively (periodic scan of a sample of expiring keys) — memory isn't immediately reclaimed when a key's TTL passes; under memory pressure, set aggressive expiry policies
- Use `OBJECT ENCODING key` to check a specific key's encoding; `MEMORY USAGE key` to see how much memory one key consumes; `MEMORY DOCTOR` for a high-level diagnosis of memory issues
